items.title: 14.1.8 Direction Angles and Direction Cosines of a Vector

blocks.title: Numbering note
blocks.text: The textbook prints this heading as 14.1.9 (Book# 14.1.9). The book has no 14.1.1, so the portal numbers the sub-headings of 14.1 in sequence as 14.1.1 to 14.1.8; 14.1.8 here is the book's 14.1.9.

Let \(\underline{r} = \underline{OP} = x\underline{i} + y\underline{j} + z\underline{k}\) be a non-zero vector, let \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) denote the angles formed between \(\underline{r}\) and the unit coordinate vectors \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\) and \(\underline{k}\) respectively, where \(0 \le \alpha \le \pi\), \(0 \le \beta \le \pi\) and \(0 \le \gamma \le \pi\).

blocks.alt: Axes x, y, z from O with short unit vectors i, j, k along them. An arrow r goes from O to a point P, with dashed lines showing its coordinates. Arcs mark the angle alpha between r and the x-axis, beta between r and the y-axis, and gamma between r and the z-axis.
blocks.caption: Direction angles α, β, γ of r = OP with i, j, k (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

items: The angles \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) are called the direction angles.
The numbers \(\cos\alpha\), \(\cos\beta\) and \(\cos\gamma\) are called direction cosines of the vector \(\underline{r}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The three angles tell how much the vector leans away from each axis. Each lies between \(0\) and \(\pi\) (\(0^{\circ}\) to \(180^{\circ}\)); an angle above \(90^{\circ}\) means that component is negative.
Example: \(\underline{r} = \underline{k}\) points straight up: \(\gamma = 0^{\circ}\), \(\alpha = \beta = 90^{\circ}\), so its direction cosines are \(0, 0, 1\).
Why the vector must be non-zero: the zero vector has no direction, so it has no direction angles.

blocks.text_alt: r equals x, y, z equals x i plus y j plus z k
therefore magnitude of r equals square root of x squared plus y squared plus z squared, which we call r

blocks.text: then \(\dfrac{\underline{r}}{|\underline{r}|} = \left[\dfrac{x}{r}, \dfrac{y}{r}, \dfrac{z}{r}\right]\) is the unit vector in the director of the vector \(\underline{r} = \underline{OP}\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "unit vector in the director of the vector"; it should read "in the direction of the vector".

blocks.alt: Axes x, y, z from O. The point P(x, y, z) is joined by solid lines to A(x, 0, 0) on the x-axis, B(0, y, 0) on the y-axis and C(0, 0, z) on the z-axis. A dashed arrow goes from O to P, and arcs mark the angles alpha, beta, gamma at O.
blocks.caption: P(x, y, z) with its feet A(x, 0, 0), B(0, y, 0), C(0, 0, z) on the axes; B is labelled (0, y, 0), see the correction (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the figure the book labels the point on the y-axis \(B(0, \gamma, 0)\). The point under discussion is the foot of \(P(x, y, z)\) on the y-axis, so it is \(B(0, y, 0)\); \(\gamma\) is an angle, not a coordinate. Our figure shows the correct label.
It can be visualized that the triangle \(OAP\) is a right triangle with \(m\angle A = 90^{\circ}\). Therefore, in right triangle \(OAP\),

blocks.text_alt: cos alpha equals OA over OP equals x over r
cos beta equals y over r, cos gamma equals z over r

blocks.alt: A right triangle O A P with the right angle at A. The horizontal side OA has length x, the hypotenuse OP is the vector r, and the angle alpha is at O.
blocks.caption: Right triangle OAP: cos α = OA/OP = x/r (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is the angle at \(A\) a right angle? \(A(x, 0, 0)\) is on the x-axis and \(\underline{AP} = [0, y, z]\) has no x-component, so \(AP\) is perpendicular to the x-axis, that is, to \(OA\). In the same way \(B\) and \(C\) give right triangles \(OBP\) and \(OCP\), which give \(\cos\beta = y/r\) and \(\cos\gamma = z/r\).
The formula \(\cos\alpha = x/r\) also holds when \(x\) is negative: then \(\alpha\) is obtuse and \(\cos\alpha < 0\).
The numbers \(\cos\alpha = \dfrac{x}{r}\), \(\cos\beta = \dfrac{y}{r}\) and \(\cos\gamma = \dfrac{z}{r}\) are called the direction cosines of \(\underline{OP}\).

blocks.text_alt: cos squared alpha plus cos squared beta plus cos squared gamma equals x squared over r squared plus y squared over r squared plus z squared over r squared
equals x squared plus y squared plus z squared over r squared equals r squared over r squared equals 1

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The direction cosines are exactly the components of the unit vector \(\hat{r}\): \(\hat{r} = \cos\alpha\,\underline{i} + \cos\beta\,\underline{j} + \cos\gamma\,\underline{k}\). Since \(\hat{r}\) has length 1, the sum of the squares of its components is 1; that is the Important Result.
Example: \(\underline{r} = 2\underline{i} - \underline{j} + 2\underline{k}\): \(r = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3\); direction cosines \(\frac{2}{3}, -\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}\). Check: \(\frac{4}{9} + \frac{1}{9} + \frac{4}{9} = 1\).
Use of the result: three angles can be direction angles of a vector only if the squares of their cosines add up to 1. For \(45^{\circ}, 45^{\circ}, 60^{\circ}\): \(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{5}{4}\), so they cannot be.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Direction angles \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\): angles of \(\underline{r}\) with \(\underline{i}, \underline{j}, \underline{k}\), each from \(0\) to \(\pi\).
Direction cosines: \(\cos\alpha = \frac{x}{r}\), \(\cos\beta = \frac{y}{r}\), \(\cos\gamma = \frac{z}{r}\), with \(r = |\underline{r}|\).
They are the components of the unit vector \(\hat{r}\).
\(\cos^{2}\alpha + \cos^{2}\beta + \cos^{2}\gamma = 1\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
Dividing by the wrong number: divide each component by the magnitude \(r\), not by the sum \(x + y + z\).
Dropping the sign: for \(x < 0\), \(\cos\alpha\) is negative and \(\alpha\) is obtuse.
Adding the cosines instead of their squares: \(\cos\alpha + \cos\beta + \cos\gamma\) is not 1 in general.
